80561.title: Incorrect S3 metadata path resolution when config is populated in Iceberg REST catalog /v1/config response
80561.feasibility_reason: The issue clearly identifies the problem area in the Iceberg REST catalog configuration parsing and metadata path resolution, specifically regarding how S3 endpoints or prefixes are handled when building absolute metadata paths. However, fixing it requires understanding the Iceberg REST client implementation and path normalization logic in ClickHouse, which can be complex.
80561.problem_summary: When reading Iceberg tables via an Iceberg REST catalog returning an 's3.endpoint' configuration, ClickHouse fails to strip the base storage path prefix from 'metadata_location', resulting in concatenated malformed S3 paths like 's3://bucket/.../s3://bucket/.../metadata.json'.
80561.root_cause_hypothesis: The relative path calculation uses a direct string comparison (`metadata_location.starts_with(data_location)`). When 's3.endpoint' is provided in the REST catalog response, 'data_location' may be normalized using the HTTP/HTTPS endpoint or bucket URL format while 'metadata_location' remains in 's3://' URI format (or vice versa). Because the scheme and host components do not match identically, the prefix check fails and the entire URI is treated as a relative key suffix.
80561.suggested_approach: Normalize both 'data_location' and 'metadata_location' by parsing them as URIs and extracting the bucket name and object key components before computing relative paths, or strip URI schemes ('s3://', 'http://', 'https://') and endpoint hostnames consistently so the bucket and relative path prefix matching succeeds.
prerequisites: Local Docker setup with MinIO and an Iceberg REST catalog (such as Apache Lakekeeper or Project Nessie) to reproduce REST config response behavior.
ClickHouse development environment capable of building and running datalake/Iceberg engine integration tests.
implementation_steps: Locate the path resolution logic where 'metadata_location' is compared against 'data_location' in the Iceberg REST catalog / storage implementation.

Implement a URI normalization helper (e.g., using `Poco::URI` or ClickHouse URI parsing utilities) to extract the bucket and key path from both 'metadata_location' and 'data_location' regardless of whether the scheme is 's3://', 'http://', or 'https://'.
Adjust the prefix matching and path stripping logic so that matching is done on the normalized S3 object key or relative table path rather than raw URI strings.
Ensure backward compatibility for catalogs that do not provide 's3.endpoint' as well as path-style versus virtual-host-style S3 endpoint configurations.
Add unit tests for path resolution and URI normalization covering various scheme and endpoint combinations.
Add integration tests using an Iceberg REST catalog (or mock REST catalog server) configured with an explicit 's3.endpoint' to verify table metadata loading.

76518.title: INSERT SELECT fails during schema inferece if the same identifier is used in projection list
76518.feasibility_reason: The issue involves schema inference during an INSERT SELECT statement where duplicate projected identifiers or expressions cause column collision errors. While reproducible with a clear example, understanding where schema inference builds the columns list for INSERT SELECT requires navigating the query execution and table block structures.
76518.problem_summary: INSERT SELECT queries against table functions (such as s3Cluster or s3) fail with ILLEGAL_COLUMN (column with this name already exists) during query analysis and schema inference when the same column identifier is projected multiple times in the SELECT clause.
76518.root_cause_hypothesis: During query analysis of table functions in QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction, schema inference inspects the SELECT projection list to determine the requested columns. When the same underlying column (e.g., `size`) is referenced multiple times with different aliases, its name is added repeatedly to a ColumnsDescription collection without deduplication or checking whether the column has already been added.
76518.suggested_approach: Deduplicate requested column names or check whether a column already exists in ColumnsDescription using `has()` before invoking `ColumnsDescription::add()` during table function schema inference and query analysis.
prerequisites: C++20 development environment configured for ClickHouse
Ability to build and run ClickHouse analyzer tests
implementation_steps: Locate the column extraction logic inside `QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction` in `src/Analyzer/QueryAnalyzer.cpp`.
Identify the loop or helper function where column names from query tree nodes are added into the `ColumnsDescription` structure for schema inference.
Update the logic to deduplicate column names or check `columns_description.has(column_name)` before calling `columns_description.add(...)`.
Add functional SQL tests in `tests/queries/0_stateless/` reproducing `INSERT INTO ... SELECT col AS x, col AS y FROM s3Cluster(...)` to prevent regressions.

58479.title: Query with broken link cannot be cancelled while reading from S3
58479.feasibility_reason: The issue describes a scenario where an S3 read operation hangs on retries with a broken link and does not check for query cancellation during the blocking network or retry loop. While the reproduction is clear, modifying the S3 client retry loops to properly respect query cancellation tokens requires careful handling of C++ threading and AWS SDK integration to avoid regressions.
58479.problem_summary: Queries reading from unreachable or broken S3 endpoints hang for long periods due to retry loops and cannot be cancelled until all retries or block generations complete.
58479.root_cause_hypothesis: Query cancellation checks and timeout limits are primarily checked between pipeline processor blocks. During S3 read operations, the thread is blocked inside the S3 storage reader (e.g., ReadBufferFromS3 or AWS SDK request/retry loops) without checking query cancellation status or passing a cancellation token to the HTTP/S3 client.
58479.suggested_approach: Inject query cancellation checks and cancellation hooks into the S3 read buffer, retry loops, and HTTP request callbacks so that network retries and blocking reads abort immediately when the query is cancelled or timed out.
prerequisites: Local ClickHouse build environment with S3 support enabled
Understanding of ClickHouse query cancellation mechanism (QueryStatus, TCPHandler, killQuery)
Understanding of ReadBufferFromS3 and AWS SDK integration in ClickHouse
implementation_steps: Trace the execution flow when initializing and reading from S3 (StorageS3, S3Source, ReadBufferFromS3, and underlying AWS SDK requests).
Identify where network retries and wait loops occur (e.g., inside ReadBufferFromS3 retry logic or custom AWS Client retry strategy).
Expose or pass the cancellation predicate / context query status (such as `is_cancelled` or `isKilled()`) down to `ReadBufferFromS3` and the retry callbacks.
Add a cancellation check before each retry attempt and during retry sleep/backoff periods to terminate early if the query was cancelled.
Ensure `ReadBufferFromS3` and `S3Source` abort gracefully by throwing an exception or returning EOF when cancellation is detected.

Add integration or functional tests (using `clickhouse-client`) verifying that a query against an unreachable S3 endpoint can be cancelled quickly via Ctrl+C / `KILL QUERY` without waiting for maximum retries.

58928.title: `kafka_skip_broken_messages` is silently ignored for `Protobuf` and `ProtobufSingle` formats
58928.feasibility_reason: The issue clearly identifies a bug where kafka_skip_broken_messages is ignored specifically for Protobuf formats in the Kafka table engine. Fixing it requires understanding how format-specific error handling interacts with the Kafka streaming reader, but it is localized to the integration between Kafka engine and the Protobuf parser.
58928.problem_summary: The `kafka_skip_broken_messages` setting is ignored when using `Protobuf` or `ProtobufSingle` formats in Kafka tables, causing queries or stream processing to throw exceptions on invalid message payloads rather than skipping them up to the set budget.
58928.root_cause_hypothesis: Exceptions thrown during Protobuf message header or payload parsing (such as length-varint decoding or field parsing in `ProtobufRowInputFormat`) bypass the broken message handling logic in `StorageKafka` or are not properly isolated per Kafka message, causing execution to terminate prematurely.
58928.suggested_approach: Audit exception propagation and input stream reset behavior in `StorageKafka` and `ProtobufRowInputFormat`. Ensure message boundary parsing failures in Protobuf formats are caught by the Kafka engine input handling loop so that broken messages increment the skipped message counter and allow consumption of subsequent valid messages.
prerequisites: Ability to build ClickHouse from source with Kafka component support.
Local test environment with integration test setup using Kafka (e.g. runner or docker-compose integration tests).
implementation_steps: Trace `StorageKafka` message reading loop to verify how broken message exceptions are handled across different format types.
Analyze `ProtobufRowInputFormat` and `ProtobufSingleRowInputFormat` exception locations during varint length parsing and protobuf deserialization.
Ensure parsing errors inside a single Kafka message trigger the `kafka_skip_broken_messages` fallback in `StorageKafka` without corrupting the stream state for subsequent Kafka messages.

Add or update integration tests in `tests/integration/` verifying that malformed Protobuf and ProtobufSingle messages are skipped up to `kafka_skip_broken_messages` while valid messages are correctly inserted.

87575.title: Lazy materialization: Method deserializeBinaryBulk of SerializationAggregateFunction does not support cases where rows_offset {} is non-zero
87575.feasibility_reason: The issue provides a clear error message, stack trace context, and reproduction schema, but implementing deserializeBinaryBulk with a non-zero rows_offset in SerializationAggregateFunction requires understanding the binary bulk deserialization protocol and how lazy materialization handles offsets for aggregate functions.
87575.problem_summary: Queries on AggregateFunction columns fail with NOT_IMPLEMENTED when lazy materialization reads data starting at a non-zero row offset within a granule.
87575.root_cause_hypothesis: `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` does not implement support for non-zero `rows_offset`, throwing `DB::Exception(ErrorCodes::NOT_IMPLEMENTED, ...)` when lazy materialization attempts to read rows starting at an offset within a mark.
87575.suggested_approach: Implement handling for `rows_offset > 0` in `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` (and `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams` if applicable) by deserializing and discarding `rows_offset` elements from the stream before deserializing `limit` rows into the destination column, or by skipping serialized states appropriately.
prerequisites: C++20 development environment configured for ClickHouse build
Understanding of ClickHouse columnar serialization (`ISerialization`, `deserializeBinaryBulk`) and AggregateFunction state deserialization
Understanding of lazy materialization reader mechanics and offsets in marks
implementation_steps: Locate `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` in `src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationAggregateFunction.cpp`.
Examine how other `ISerialization` implementations handle non-zero `rows_offset` when deserializing bulk streams.

Update `SerializationAggregateFunction::deserializeBinaryBulk` so that when `rows_offset > 0`, it allocates a temporary AggregateFunction state (or uses temporary memory) and deserializes/destroys `rows_offset` items to advance the read stream.

Ensure `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams` or any relevant stream reading helpers in `SerializationAggregateFunction` properly propagate and handle `rows_offset` without throwing `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`.
Add a regression test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/` using the reproduction query with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT ... OFFSET` and `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization = 1`.

58662.title: Support defaults in Native format
58662.feasibility_reason: The issue requests adding a new data format 'NativeWithDefaults' similar to an existing 'RowBinaryWithDefaults' format. While the pattern exists elsewhere in the codebase, implementing a new format in ClickHouse involves deep C++ knowledge of serialization/deserialization routines, block processing, and format registries.
blockers: Requires understanding the complex ClickHouse block input/output and format serialization internals.
58662.problem_summary: ClickHouse's Native format currently requires all column values to be provided explicitly on the client side, making it impossible to let the server evaluate default expressions during insertion in Native format.
58662.root_cause_hypothesis: The Native input format strictly deserializes blocks containing full columns matching the provided structure and does not provide a mechanism to fill in omitted columns using server-side default expressions, unlike formats like RowBinaryWithDefaults.
58662.suggested_approach: Implement a new format 'NativeWithDefaults' (modeled after RowBinaryWithDefaults) by creating or adapting Native format processors that read incoming Native blocks with a subset of columns and evaluate server-side defaults for any missing columns based on table metadata.
prerequisites: Familiarity with ClickHouse's Native block serialization format
Understanding of ClickHouse IInputFormat / IOutputFormat processors and FormatFactory registration
Review of PR/issue #50854 (RowBinaryWithDefaults) for the defaults evaluation pattern via evaluateMissingDefaults
implementation_steps: Review the implementation of RowBinaryWithDefaultsBlockInputFormat and how it utilizes ActionsDAG / evaluateMissingDefaults to populate missing columns.
Add format registration for 'NativeWithDefaults' in FormatFactory (with appropriate FormatSettings flags or dedicated input/output format classes).

Implement NativeWithDefaultsBlockInputFormat inheriting from or wrapping NativeBlockInputFormat, modifying block reading so that columns missing in the input stream are generated and filled according to table default expressions.
Ensure NativeWithDefaults handles cases where block column headers differ from the expected schema by filling missing columns and correctly ignoring/reordering columns if needed.
Optionally implement NativeWithDefaultsBlockOutputFormat if output behavior needs to distinguish default handling, or alias it to standard Native output format.
Write comprehensive stateless tests in tests/queries/0_stateless to verify inserting tables with default, materialized, and alias columns using FORMAT NativeWithDefaults.
Add documentation for NativeWithDefaults format under docs/en/interfaces/formats/.

65251.title: Replicated database: Stuck DDL after a failed DROP DATABASE
65251.feasibility_reason: The issue describes a filesystem error (File name too long) when dropping a database containing a table with an extremely long name, leading to a stuck DDL log in ZooKeeper/Keeper. While reproducible, it requires understanding the DDL queue handling for Replicated databases and how errors during DROP DATABASE affect the state machine.
65251.problem_summary: In Replicated database engine, dropping a database containing a table with a name near the filesystem limit causes a 'File name too long' error when moving metadata to metadata_dropped. This leaves the DDL worker thread stopped and permanently wedges the DDL queue even across restarts.
65251.root_cause_hypothesis: When dropping a table or database, ClickHouse moves table metadata to `metadata_dropped/<database>.<table_name>.<uuid>.sql`. Appending the database name, table UUID, and extension exceeds the filesystem limit (typically 255 bytes / NAME_MAX) for long table names. During `DROP DATABASE` execution in `DatabaseReplicated`, the DDL worker stops (`stop_flag = true`) in anticipation of database destruction. When the drop fails with an exception, the stop state is not reverted and the DDL task remains stuck in the queue, causing an unrecoverable failure loop on restart.
65251.suggested_approach: Two-pronged fix: 1) Ensure metadata filenames in `metadata_dropped` never exceed `NAME_MAX` by truncating/hashing long prefixes or using just the UUID; 2) Improve exception handling in `DatabaseReplicated` DDL execution so that transient or failed DROP operations do not permanently leave the DDL worker stopped or wedged in an infinite retry loop without recovery.
prerequisites: A local ClickHouse development environment with Keeper / ZooKeeper enabled to test Replicated databases
Familiarity with DatabaseCatalog metadata handling, `metadata_dropped`, and DatabaseReplicated DDL queue execution
implementation_steps: Investigate `DatabaseCatalog::enqueueDatabaseDropped` and `DatabaseCatalog::enqueueTableDropped` (or equivalent metadata_dropped path generation) to inspect how destination filenames are formatted.

Introduce truncation or hashing of the table/database name component when generating destination paths in `metadata_dropped` so the filename strictly fits within 255 bytes (e.g., `<uuid>.sql` or truncated `<escaped_name>.<uuid>.sql`).
Alternatively or additionally, ensure table name length checks at creation account for the overhead of the `.metadata_dropped` suffix / uuid, or enforce NAME_MAX constraints consistently.

Examine `DatabaseReplicated::drop` and `DatabaseReplicatedDDLWorker`: ensure that if `DROP DATABASE` throws an exception, `stop_flag` is reset or the worker is recovered/re-initialized if the database is not actually dropped.

Check how DDL queue processing in `DatabaseReplicatedDDLWorker` handles fatal metadata errors so that the replication queue can either log a fatal error / mark the task failed or be resumed rather than permanently deadlocking all DDL operations.

Add an integration test creating a Replicated database, creating a table with a name near the character limit, executing `DROP DATABASE`, and asserting that it either drops successfully or fails gracefully without stopping replication/DDLs.

71793.title: Deletion Error with Ephemeral Column in Table
71793.feasibility_reason: The issue provides clear reproduction steps and points to a missing column error during mutations/deletions on tables containing ephemeral columns. However, understanding how ephemeral columns are handled during mutations in mutations/mutation engine logic might require deeper codebase familiarity.
71793.problem_summary: Executing lightweight DELETE queries on a table with a MATERIALIZED column depending on an EPHEMERAL column fails with an UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER error for the EPHEMERAL column.
71793.root_cause_hypothesis: Lightweight DELETE planning (likely in InterpreterDeleteQuery or mutation pipeline construction) unnecessarily includes or evaluates default/materialized column expressions when constructing the pipeline for filtering or mutating `_row_exists`. Because EPHEMERAL columns are not physically stored in parts, evaluating the MATERIALIZED column expression fails due to missing source columns.
71793.suggested_approach: Ensure that lightweight DELETE query planning only resolves columns required by the WHERE clause and the internal row-tracking columns (such as `_row_exists`), avoiding redundant expansion or calculation of MATERIALIZED/DEFAULT column DAGs that depend on EPHEMERAL or non-existent columns.
prerequisites: Local ClickHouse development environment capable of building and running clickhouse-server and clickhouse-client.
Understanding of lightweight delete execution path and column dependency resolution in ClickHouse.
implementation_steps: Reproduce the bug using a stateless test script in `tests/queries/0_stateless/` with a MergeTree table having an EPHEMERAL column and a MATERIALIZED column depending on it, then executing a `DELETE FROM <table> WHERE ...` query.
Trace the stack trace of the `Missing columns: 'IDEphemereal' while processing query` error using a debug build or `gdb` during execution of `DELETE FROM`.

Inspect the query analysis and pipeline preparation in `InterpreterDeleteQuery` and the underlying mutation interpreter to identify where materialized/default column expressions are being analyzed or added to the execution DAG.

Modify the mutation/delete header and expression building logic so that materialized column expressions are skipped when the operation only updates `_row_exists` or does not mutate those specific columns.
Verify that `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE`, regular `DELETE FROM`, and `INSERT` still work properly and preserve expected materialized column semantics.
Add a functional test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/` validating `DELETE FROM` on tables with EPHEMERAL and dependent MATERIALIZED columns.

11942.title: allow_ddl option is not consistent over restarts
11942.feasibility_reason: The issue involves configuration persistence and profile settings for DDL operations across server restarts, which requires tracing how profile settings are stored, loaded, and initialized upon startup compared to on-the-fly reloads. While reproducible via a provided script, ClickHouse server configuration and user profiles subsystem can be complex.
11942.problem_summary: Setting 'allow_ddl = 0' in the default profile prevents subsequent DDL operations across all profiles after a server restart, particularly affecting asynchronous/ON CLUSTER queries executed by background workers.
11942.root_cause_hypothesis: Background DDL execution (such as DDLWorker processing tasks from ZooKeeper for ON CLUSTER queries, or internal startup DDL routines) uses an internal execution context derived from the server's global context or the default profile. When 'allow_ddl' is disabled in the default profile, the DDLWorker inherits this restriction upon server restart, causing distributed or background DDL queries to fail regardless of the initiating user's profile settings.
11942.suggested_approach: Ensure that internal execution contexts used by DDLWorker (and any internal server query execution routines) explicitly set 'allow_ddl = 1' or bypass the client-facing 'allow_ddl' setting check, as authorization has already been verified at the entrypoint of the query.
prerequisites: Working ClickHouse build and test environment (C++20/cmake/ninja).
Local ClickHouse cluster or ZooKeeper instance capable of executing ON CLUSTER DDL queries.
implementation_steps: Reproduce the issue by creating a custom profile with allow_ddl = 1, setting allow_ddl = 0 in the default profile, executing an ON CLUSTER DDL query, and restarting clickhouse-server.
Examine DDLWorker.cpp where task execution context is created (e.g., `DDLWorker::processTask` or `createContextForQuery`) and inspect how settings are initialized.

Explicitly override `settings.allow_ddl = true` (or `setSetting("allow_ddl", 1)`) on the context created for executing DDL worker tasks, or adjust the context creation logic to not inherit restrictive default user profile settings for internal DDL processing.

Verify whether other background or system queries (like table loading/reattaching on startup) are affected by default profile settings and ensure internal contexts have necessary operational permissions.

Add an integration test (e.g., in `tests/integration/test_ddl_worker/`) that configures the default profile with allow_ddl = 0, restarts the server, and verifies that distributed DDL queries from authorized profiles succeed.
